q: Why isn't POS tagging just dictionary lookup?
short: Many frequent words have several tags (book NN/VB, back JJ/NN/RB/VB); the correct tag depends on context, so lookup (the unigram baseline) plateaus around 90–92%.
follow: What does the baseline get wrong?

q: Why add character-level embeddings?
short: They build a representation from spelling, so unseen or rare words still get informative vectors (suffixes -ly, -ing, -tion; capitalisation), concatenated with the word vector.
mistakes: Assigning OOV words a zero vector.

q: What do the LSTM gates do?
short: Forget gate decides how much of the old cell to keep, input gate how much new candidate content to write, output gate how much of the cell to expose as h; this lets information persist across long spans.
detail: c = f⊙c + i⊙g; h = o⊙tanh c.
follow: Why does this help vanishing gradients?

q: Why use a Bi-LSTM for tagging?
short: A tag can depend on words to the right as well as the left; a backward LSTM supplies right context and concatenating both gives each token a full-sentence representation.
detail: Can't be used for left-to-right generation.
mistakes: Using a unidirectional encoder for tagging.

q: What does the CRF layer add on top of a Bi-LSTM?
short: Learned tag-to-tag transition scores and global normalisation over sequences, so the decoder (Viterbi) picks the best consistent sequence rather than independent per-token maxima.
detail: Training uses the forward algorithm for Z.
follow: Is it still needed with BERT?

q: Why does 97% per-token accuracy matter less than it sounds?
short: For 20-word sentences, 0.97²⁰ ≈ 0.544 are fully correct; at 99%, 0.818. Per million tokens, 30,000 vs 10,000 errors.

q: How do you fine-tune BERT for POS tagging?
short: Tokenise into subwords, run BERT, apply a linear layer to each token's final vector (one logit per tag), use cross-entropy on the first subword of each word, and train the whole model for a few epochs with a small learning rate.
detail: Ignore non-first pieces in the loss.

q: Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting for tagging?
short: Zero-shot gives only instructions and may drift from the tagset (ADJ vs JJ); few-shot adds examples in the exact format so the model copies the convention. Neither updates weights.

q: Compute the CRF best path and probability for 'the plays'.
short: Path scores E₁ + T + E₂: DT NN = 5 + 4 + 2 = 11 (best), DT VBZ = 7, NN VBZ = 6 … Z ≈ 61,402.9 → P(DT NN) = e¹¹/Z ≈ 0.975; P(DT VBZ) ≈ 0.018.
follow: How would Z be computed for long sentences?
mistakes: Forgetting to include all nine paths in Z.

Bi-LSTM-CRF vs fine-tuned Transformer taggers?
short: Bi-LSTM-CRF: sequential, slower to train, ~97–98%, good with limited compute and data. Transformers: parallel over positions, pre-trained knowledge, ~98.5–99.5%, heavier at inference and O(n²) attention.

q: What risks come with LLM prompting for tagging?
short: Inconsistent or off-tagset labels, hallucinated tags, tokenisation mismatches with your pipeline, nondeterminism, cost and latency at scale, and privacy concerns when sending text to an external API.
detail: Mitigate with few-shot, constrained output, validation.

q: Describe an agentic pipeline that uses a tagger.
short: The LLM reads the request, decomposes it, calls a tagging tool where precise labels are needed, parses the tool output, and continues (e.g. pairing nouns with adjectives for aspect sentiment), finally writing the answer.
detail: Division of labour: planning vs precision.
mistakes: Letting the LLM tag thousands of reviews itself.

q: How do contextual embeddings change tagging?
short: BERT gives each occurrence its own vector depending on the sentence, so ambiguous words are separated before classification; a linear head then suffices, unlike static embeddings that need a contextual encoder on top.

q: Choose a tagging approach for 50 million social-media posts per day.
short: Fine-tune a compact Transformer (distilled) on in-domain annotated posts (normalisation for hashtags, emojis, code-mixing), possibly with LLM-assisted annotation; batch on GPUs; monitor accuracy on a weekly sample; avoid per-post LLM calls for cost.

q: Why might a CRF layer help less on top of BERT than on top of a Bi-LSTM?
short: Self-attention already lets each token's representation depend on neighbouring decisions' evidence, so per-token softmax is usually consistent; CRFs still help where label constraints are strict (BIO tags in NER).

q: How does the partition function Z make CRFs globally normalised, and why does it matter?
short: Z sums exp(score) over all sequences, so probabilities compare whole sequences; a locally poor transition lowers the whole path's probability, avoiding MEMM label bias. Z is computed in O(N²n) by the forward algorithm.

q: Build a tagger for a low-resource language with 500 labelled sentences.
short: Start from a multilingual pre-trained Transformer (e.g. XLM-R), fine-tune on the 500 sentences with UD tags, add character features or a CRF if helpful, use cross-lingual transfer from related languages, few-shot LLM annotation plus human correction for more data, and evaluate on held-out sentences.

q: Is POS tagging 'solved'?
short: On clean, in-domain benchmark text, fine-tuned Transformers approach annotator agreement (~99%). It is not solved for noisy domains, code-mixed text, low-resource languages, or sentence-level correctness; and the practical question has shifted to using tags inside larger systems.
follow: What would convince you it's solved?
